references.title: University Physics Volume 1, 16.2 Mathematics of Waves
observedTextSections: Modeling a One-Dimensional Sinusoidal Wave using a Wave Function
primaryRelationsObserved: A constant-shape disturbance moves by v times the elapsed time.
The sinusoidal string model has constant A and period T.
The model uses k=2*pi/lambda, omega=2*pi/T and phase k*x-omega*t+phi for rightward propagation.
A wave advances one wavelength per period, giving v=lambda/T=omega/k.
reviewerDerivationsNotFigureObservations: At a fixed time, a separation lambda changes phase by 2*pi; the nearest distinct same-phase points along propagation are one wavelength apart.
A separation lambda/2 changes phase by pi and reverses both displacement and instantaneous oscillatory velocity.
At fixed position the period is T; at fixed time the spatial period is lambda.
Using frequency nu=1/T gives v=lambda*nu; translating the pattern by Delta s requires Delta t=Delta s/v.

references.title: University Physics Volume 1, 16.1 Traveling Waves
references.urlBasis: Sibling section linked in the publisher navigation; web searches returned no surfaced results
primaryRelationsObserved: A wave is a propagating disturbance; basic mechanical waves require a medium.
Mechanical waves transfer energy and momentum while medium particles oscillate about equilibrium rather than transporting mass with the wave.
Frequency is the reciprocal of period, and wave speed equals wavelength divided by period.
The text distinguishes transverse and longitudinal mechanical-wave motion and gives examples of both.
